title: Space Debris: Junk in Orbit

segments.say: Nobody knows what this object is. It was photographed from the space station, one of countless bits of orbiting junk.
Space debris is anything up there that no longer works: dead satellites, spent rocket stages, fragments, even flecks of paint.
The US Space Surveillance Network has catalogued more than thirty-four thousand objects. It tracks pieces bigger than about ten centimetres; smaller ones mostly go unseen.
In low orbit, debris moves at seven to eight kilometres a second. Crashes happen at about ten on average, so even a tiny piece hits hard.
These pits were made by tiny particles, on a panel that NASA brought back from orbit.

items.text: a weather satellite destroyed on purpose

segments.say: Two events made it much worse: a satellite destroyed on purpose in two thousand and seven, and an accidental crash in two thousand and nine.

anim.title: Living with it
items: The ISS dodges if the risk is above 1 in 10,000
Below 600 km, debris falls back within years

segments.say: The space station dodges when the risk of a hit tops one in ten thousand. Below six hundred kilometres, debris falls back within years.
For GS Three, link this to space sustainability: where dead hardware is left decides how long it stays.

sources: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, FAQ (orbitaldebris.jsc.nasa.gov/faq): kinds of debris (derelict spacecraft, upper stages, fragments from explosions and collisions, paint flecks); the US Space Surveillance Network had catalogued more than 34,000 objects; routinely tracks objects larger than about 10 cm; debris in low Earth orbit travels at 7–8 km/s; average impact speed about 10 km/s, up to about 15 km/s; Fengyun-1C destruction (2007) and Iridium 33–Cosmos 2251 collision (2009) greatly increased large debris; the ISS manoeuvres when collision risk exceeds 1 in 10,000 (41 times since 1999); debris below 600 km normally falls back within several years

quiz.q: About how fast does debris travel in low Earth orbit?
quiz.why: NASA ODPO: about 7 to 8 km per second.

quiz.q: What size of object does the US network routinely track?
quiz.why: Routine tracking covers objects bigger than about 10 cm.

quiz.q: What happens to debris below about 600 km?
options: It stays for millions of years
It is collected by the ISS
It normally falls back within several years
quiz.why: Air drag pulls low debris down within several years.

reviewNote: All facts are from the NASA ODPO FAQ. Countries are not named on purpose. Moving facts: the catalogued count (34,000+) and the ISS manoeuvre count rise over time; the count of manoeuvres is left out of the script. No India angle was sourced in time; ISRO's debris-free missions goal could be added with a PIB source.
